chapter: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
title: Manuel Moneta, Turk Rene's range and Al Hirt
summary: The interviewer took lessons from Manuel Moneta, who taught Hardy and Rene. Brownlee describes Rene's reading and high notes, and compares Al Hirt's range.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: Well, I know his brother, and, uh, uh, Manuel Moneta. Do you know Manuel Moneta?
Yes, he lived, he lived in Algiers.
Well, I took lessons from him, you know.
Is that right?
Since he taught Emmett Hardy and, and all those guys.
Yeah.
I decided I'd take lessons from him.
And he taught me a lot about René.
He taught René, too, some of those, you know, after René was playing.

Well, Turk René, Turk René in those days, a lot of the, a lot of the musicians didn't bother about reading. Mm-hmm. But, uh, Turk always read. He could always read his music. And, uh, I hear him going up for screaming notes, and I've heard Turk make some of the clearest, finest high notes I've ever, of any trumpet man.
Do you estimate how high he would go up and still get a good tone?
E, and sometimes F. Broad, wide open, fine.
That's above the staff?
Oh, yeah. That's very...
I'm trying to figure out which line it would be. That'd be the...
Well, now...
The E, the third line above the staff?
Yeah. Four... Above, yeah. Third above.
Third above.
Uh... Oh, am I right? I don't know.
Yeah, that's right.
Yeah.
That's... Yeah. He'd go up there and still have a beautiful tone.

Nice, fine tone. Uh... Well, Al Hurt is another one can do... Does that. Al can take any... Any number he plays, he'll go from... Uh, in my... My way of listening, he goes from low G to... High G above. There's no head to him. I think he masters his horn very well.
